A Syrian bishop known for his role in the conflict that led to the downfall of John Chrysostom. After gaining popularity as a preacher in Constantinople, he became involved in political and ecclesiastical intrigues against Chrysostom, aligning with Empress Eudoxia and participating in the accusations at the Synod of the Oak. A number of his sermons survive, including homilies on Genesis and the creation of the world.

column25: Bishop of Rome from 269 to 274. He is said to have corresponded with Domnus of Antioch and Maximus of Alexandria during controversies surrounding Paul of Samosata.

A Greek philosopher, historian, and biographer whose life is known mainly from remarks in his own writings. A Platonist thinker and priest at Delphi, he wrote extensively on ethics, religion, and philosophy in the collection known as the Moralia, and is best known for the Parallel Lives, a series of paired biographies comparing Greek and Roman statesmen.

A Greek satirist and rhetorician from Samosata on the Euphrates. He described himself as a Syrian and rose from humble origins to become a prominent writer of the Second Sophistic. After training in rhetoric and traveling widely as a public speaker, he composed many satirical dialogues that mock philosophy, religion, and social pretensions with sharp wit and skepticism.

A pagan philosopher, rhetorician, and statesman active in Constantinople. He served emperors from Constantius II to Theodosius I and later as prefect of the city. Educated in philosophy with a strong engagement with Aristotle, he combined public oratory with philosophical thought and wrote orations and Aristotelian commentaries.

A physician and teacher of medicine associated with the Gaza school of sophists in the late 5th–early 6th century CE. A student of the Jewish physician Domnos, he was initially hostile to Christianity and mocked Christian healing shrines, though he was later baptized and appears in accounts connected with the cult of Saints Cyrus and John at Menuthis.

column25: Traditionally regarded as the author of the Iliad and Odyssey. His life and identity are uncertain in antiquity and reconstructed from later traditions. Ancient sources variously associated him with cities such as Smyrna and Chios and developed biographical legends about his origin and career as a poet.

A prominent representative of Hellenistic-Jewish philosophy in Alexandria who sought to interpret the Hebrew Scriptures through Greek philosophical traditions, especially Platonism and Stoicism. A member of a wealthy and influential Jewish family, he is known for his allegorical commentaries on the Pentateuch and for leading a Jewish embassy to the emperor Caligula to protest anti-Jewish measures in Alexandria.

Traditionally regarded as the founder of Attic philosophy. His life and teaching are difficult to reconstruct because of conflicting ancient traditions and later interpretations. He was remembered as the son of Sophroniscus and Phainarete, as a public opponent of injustice, and as the philosopher whose trial and execution in 399 BCE made him one of antiquity’s defining intellectual figures.

column25: Bishop of Samosata around 431. He is remembered as a principled defender of Antiochene Christology against the Cyrillian position, and only his letters survive.
An Egyptian monk of the Nitrian Desert, remembered in monastic tradition as a disciple of Antony. He was a noted ascetic of early Egyptian monasticism and was visited by Melania the Elder.

Roman procurator of Judea from 26–36 CE and best known in Christian tradition as the official who presided over the trial of Jesus. In the New Testament he appears primarily in the passion narratives, with additional references in Luke, Acts, and 1 Timothy, reflecting his enduring role in early Christian memory of Jesus’s death.

An Athenian orator, teacher, and prose stylist whose rhetorical vision helped shape classical Greek education and civic discourse; his surviving works include political speeches, educational essays, and letters. Trained among the leading intellectual circles of his age, he founded an influential school of rhetoric and became one of antiquity’s central theorists of paideia and public speech.

Menander was an Athenian comic poet of the New Comedy, probably born in 343/2 BCE and educated in the circle of Theophrastus. Ancient biographical tradition presents him as highly gifted and prolific, though only modestly successful in dramatic competitions during his lifetime. After his death, his reputation rose greatly, and later scholars treated him as a major literary authority.

column25: An Alexandrian mathematician of the early Hellenistic period, probably active under Ptolemy I. He was a leading representative of a mathematical school in Alexandria, best known for the Elements, the foundational synthesis of ancient geometry, which organized earlier Greek mathematics into a systematic work that remained the standard textbook for centuries.

An Ionian Greek philosopher and polymath from Samos and founder of Pythagoreanism. He was associated with a community that combined religious teaching, communal and ascetic life, , and belief in immortality and transmigration. The tradition surrounding him generated a wide body of sacred books, hypomnemata, and later pseudepigraphic writings.

An Athenian philosopher, born in the late fifth century BCE, and a devoted follower of Socrates. He founded the Academy, the school from which Platonism took its name. Ancient tradition presented him as a supremely wise and divinely favored teacher, and through biographies, dialogues, letters, and the school that continued after him, he became the central figure of the Platonic tradition.

A bishop of Caesarea in Palestine around 390, probably a nephew of Cyril of Jerusalem, and was regarded as a learned and rhetorically polished theologian in the tradition of mediating Nicene orthodoxy. He wrote against the Anomoeans and was also associated with the Greek transmission of Rufinus’ church history, though the exact extent of his authorship remains uncertain.

Bishop of Ptolemais in Palestine around 400 CE. He was renowned as an orator and for a time enjoyed great acclaim in Constantinople, where he became one of Chrysostom’s fiercest opponents. He wrote homilies as well as a large work against avarice.

A Greek historian associated in later tradition with an early Greek version of Rome’s foundation legend, especially the story of Romulus and Remus. Although later antiquarian sources treat him as an important authority for the received narrative, his precise role remains uncertain, and the surviving excerpt attributed to him ends with the fall of Amulius rather than the founding of Rome.

A Bishop of Jerusalem from 386 to 417, successor of Cyril, and was known as an eloquent preacher, learned theologian, and supporter of monasticism. He became prominent through his involvement in the Origenist and Pelagian controversies, yet remained respected as an orthodox authority.

column25: A second-century Christian apologist and martyr who presented Christianity as the true philosophy, drawing on his earlier training in pagan philosophical schools, especially Platonism. Active at Rome in the mid-second century, he is known above all for his two Apologies and the Dialogue with Trypho, and he was executed under the urban prefect Junius Rusticus.
